mainTopic: Careful questioning in money cases, the meaning of 'צדק צדק תרדף', and how בית דין opens a capital case in favor of the accused.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a side question: if money cases are judged in a relaxed way, should judges who make mistakes be excused from paying? The גמרא says no, because that would scare off lenders even more. Next, the גמרא resolves why our משנה requires careful questioning (דרישה וחקירה) in money cases when other sources do not. רבא says our משנה is about fines (קנסות). רב פפא says it is about a case that looks suspicious (דין מרומה), and he matches the view of ריש לקיש, who read the double 'צדק צדק תרדף' the same way. רב אשי instead reads the double 'justice' as one for strict דין and one for פשרה. A ברייתא supports him with the picture of two boats and two camels that must take turns. Two more ברייתות read the same פסוק as a call to seek out the best בית דין and the great חכמים in their towns. Finally, the גמרא asks what words בית דין uses to open a capital case in favor of the accused. רב יהודה's and עולא's wordings are rejected. רבה, רב כהנא, אביי and רבא, and רב אשי each give a wording, and a ברייתא from the סוטה ceremony begins to support אביי and רבא; that proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Should mistaken judges be excused from paying?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that money cases are judged in a relaxed way: if so, judges who make a mistake should not have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the judges made a mistake, should they not have to pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back on the idea that money cases skip careful questioning of witnesses. It asks: if the court was told to go easy, shouldn't judges who get it wrong be excused from paying?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא explained that money cases skip דרישה וחקירה so that lenders keep lending. The challenge is: if judges are not allowed to question witnesses carefully, they can say a mistake wasn't their fault. So why should they ever pay for a wrong ruling?

keyTerms.meaning: Careful questioning of the witnesses about the details of their testimony

steps.confusionAlert: This line starts in the middle of an argument. The words just before it (at the end of the previous amud) set up the idea that money cases are judged in a relaxed way. This question is built on that idea.

phrases.english: If they erred, should they not pay?
phrases.notes: "They" means the judges. If their ruling caused someone to lose money, normally they have to pay it back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from the previous amud about why money cases skip דרישה וחקירה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning that money cases are relaxed so as not to 'lock the door before borrowers'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the court is told not to examine witnesses closely, a judge's mistake is not his fault, so he should be free from paying.

steps.title: Excusing judges would scare lenders even more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that excusing mistaken judges would hurt lenders even more, which is the very thing the rule is trying to prevent.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the more so, you would be locking the door in front of borrowers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. If judges did not have to pay for their mistakes, people would be even more afraid to lend money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole reason for relaxing money cases is to keep lenders lending. If lenders knew a wrong ruling could cost them their money with no one to pay it back, they would stop lending. So the same reason that relaxes the questioning also requires judges to pay for their mistakes.

keyTerms.meaning: Locking the door in front of borrowers: making people afraid to lend

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the concern for keeping loans available is a basic policy that shapes several rules in money cases.

phrases.english: All the more so
you would lock the door in front of borrowers!

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁתִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לוֹוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turns the challenger's own reason around: the same concern for lenders requires judges to pay.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the court is relaxed in money cases, judges should be excused for mistakes.
steps.terutzMaskana: Excusing judges would hurt lenders even more, so judges still pay for their mistakes.

steps.title: רבא: our משנה is about fines, the others are about loans
steps.stepSummary: רבא resolves the contradiction by saying our משנה, which requires careful questioning, is about fines, while the other sources are about admissions and loans.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Our משנה here is talking about fines, and the other sources are talking about admissions and loans.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא goes back to the main contradiction and solves it. He says the sources are talking about different kinds of money cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fines (קנסות) are payments set by the תורה that go beyond the actual damage, so the court is extra careful and questions witnesses closely. Admissions and loans are everyday cases where the concern for lenders applies, so the court is relaxed. That way both sources are true, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: Fines: fixed payments set by the תורה, beyond the actual loss
Admissions: cases where someone admits he owes money

phrases.english: Rava said:
Our משנה here is about cases of fines,
and the other is about admissions and loans.
phrases.notes: "The other" means the sources that said money cases skip careful questioning.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר מַתְנִיתִין דְּהָכָא בְּדִינֵי קְנָסוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side question is settled, the גמרא returns to the main contradiction between the sources.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: different kinds of money cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה and the other sources disagree about all money cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fines need careful questioning; admissions and loans do not.

steps.title: רב פפא: it depends on whether the case looks suspicious
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says all the sources are about admissions and loans; careful questioning is needed only when the case looks like it may be a fraud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Both sources are about admissions and loans. Here it is a case that looks like a fraud; there it is a case that does not look like a fraud.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא offers a different solution to the same contradiction. He says the difference is not the type of case but whether the court suspects trickery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא agrees that the other sources are about admissions and loans, but he says our משנה is about them too. When the court suspects one side is cheating, perhaps with lying witnesses, it must question the witnesses carefully. When nothing looks wrong, the court stays relaxed so lenders are not scared off.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one: both sources
A case that looks like a fraud or trick

steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא is not adding to רבא's answer in step 3. He is giving his own, different answer to the same contradiction.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Both this and that are about an admission and a loan.
Here, it is about a case that looks fraudulent,
phrases.notes: "Here" means our משנה, which requires careful questioning.

phrases.english: there, it is about a case that does not look fraudulent.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּהוֹדָאָה וְהַלְוָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the contradiction that רבא answered in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases by whether there is suspicion of fraud, not by the type of claim.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference must be the kind of case, such as fines versus loans.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even in loans, a case that looks suspicious needs careful questioning; a normal case does not.

steps.title: ריש לקיש points out two פסוקים that seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רב פפא's idea matches ריש לקיש, who pointed out a contradiction between two פסוקים about judging with justice.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like ריש לקיש, because ריש לקיש pointed out a contradiction: It is written, 'In justice you shall judge your fellow,' and it is written, 'Justice, justice you shall pursue.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רב פפא from ריש לקיש. This step sets up ריש לקיש's question, and the next step will give his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One פסוק says 'justice' once, and the other says it twice. The doubled word suggests a higher level of care than normal judging. ריש לקיש asks how the two fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: He points out a contradiction (literally, 'he throws' two sources against each other)

phrases.english: This is like Reish Lakish,
for Reish Lakish raised a contradiction:
It is written: "In justice you shall judge your fellow,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:15

phrases.english: and it is written: "Justice, justice you shall pursue."
phrases.notes: דברים 16:20

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces ריש לקיש's teaching as support for רב פפא's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים about justice in judging.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says 'justice' once and the other says it twice, so they seem to require different levels of care.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's answer: suspicious case versus normal case
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that the double 'justice' is for a case that looks fraudulent, and the single 'justice' is for a normal case, which is exactly רב פפא's distinction.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can this be? Here it is about a case that looks fraudulent; there it is about a case that does not look fraudulent.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש settles the clash between the פסוקים. In doing so, he gives the same distinction רב פפא used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Justice, justice' (said twice) means the judge must take extra care when a case looks suspicious. 'In justice' (said once) is enough for a normal case. This gives רב פפא's answer a basis in the פסוקים: extra questioning only when there is a smell of fraud.

keyTerms.meaning: How can this be? (how do the two fit together)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers to why our משנה requires careful questioning in money cases when other sources do not. רבא: our משנה is about fines (קנסות), and the others are about admissions and loans. רב פפא: all are about loans, but a suspicious case (דין מרומה) needs careful questioning, which matches ריש לקיש's reading of 'צדק צדק תרדף'.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a judge's level of care depends on the situation: when something seems off, the court must dig deeper.

phrases.english: How can this be?
Here, it is about a case that looks fraudulent,
phrases.notes: "Here" means the double "justice, justice" פסוק, which calls for extra care.

phrases.english: there, it is about a case that does not look fraudulent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's question from step 5, which supports רב פפא from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: suspicious case versus normal case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים contradict each other about how carefully to judge.
steps.terutzMaskana: The double 'justice' is for suspicious cases and the single 'justice' is for normal ones, which supports רב פפא.

steps.title: רב אשי: one 'justice' for judgment, one for compromise
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the משנה can be explained by the earlier answers. The two פסוקים are not about fraud versus normal cases. One is about strict judgment and one is about compromise.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Our משנה is explained the way we already answered. As for the verses, one is about strict judgment and one is about compromise.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different way to solve ריש לקיש's contradiction between the two פסוקים about 'justice'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי does not need the fraud-case reading to explain our משנה, because the answers the גמרא already gave handle it. So he is free to read the two פסוקים differently. The double 'justice' covers two kinds of fairness: דין (strict law) and פשרה (compromise).

keyTerms.meaning: As we answered (by the earlier answers)
Strict judgment by the letter of the law

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not arguing with the earlier explanations of the משנה. He only gives a new reading of the two פסוקים.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Our Mishnah is as we answered,
and the verses: one is for judgment
phrases.notes: These are the two פסוקים about 'justice' that ריש לקיש set against each other.

phrases.english: and one is for compromise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different resolution to ריש לקיש's contradiction than the fraud/normal distinction of Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the verses: the two mentions of 'justice' refer to two different kinds of fairness, not two kinds of cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The double 'justice' must be for a case that looks fraudulent.
steps.terutzMaskana: The double 'justice' teaches both strict judgment and compromise, and the משנה is explained by the earlier answers.

steps.title: Support from a ברייתא: two boats and two camels
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that 'justice, justice' means one for judgment and one for compromise. It shows this with two boats on a narrow river and two camels on a narrow path.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'Justice, justice you shall pursue.' One is for judgment and one is for compromise. How so? Two boats are sailing on a river and meet each other. If both try to pass at once, both sink. If they go one after the other, both get through. The same is true of two camels climbing the narrow ascent of בית חורון that meet each other. If both climb at once, both fall. If they go one after the other, both make it up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רב אשי said. It gives a picture of why compromise is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here strict law cannot help, because neither boat has a better legal right to go first. If each side insists on its full right, both lose everything. Only an arrangement where one waits lets both succeed, and that is the 'justice' of compromise.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא
The steep, narrow climb of בית חורון

phrases.english: As it is taught in a baraita:
"Justice, justice you shall pursue" –
phrases.notes: דברים 16:20

phrases.english: one is for judgment and one is for compromise.
How so?
Two boats are traveling on the river
and they meet each other;
if both pass at once, both sink;
one after the other, both pass.
And similarly, two camels
that were climbing the ascent of Beit Horon
and they meet each other;
if both climb at once, both fall;
one after the other, both climb up.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְתַנְיָא: צֶדֶק צֶדֶק תִּרְדֹּף אֶחָד לְדִין וְאֶחָד לִפְשָׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that states רב אשי's reading word for word.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's reading that the double 'justice' means judgment and compromise.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on 'צדק צדק תרדף' with the examples of the boats and the camels.

steps.title: How to decide who goes first
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains who goes first. A loaded boat goes before an empty one. One that is far from its destination goes before one that is close. If they are equal, they make a compromise and the one going first pays the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does this work? If one boat is loaded and one is not, the unloaded one gives way to the loaded one. If one is close to its destination and one is not, the close one gives way to the one that is not close. If both are close or both are far, set up a compromise between them, and they pay each other for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and lays out the practical rules for deciding which side yields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rules give priority to the side that would lose more by waiting. A loaded boat is harder to hold back, and a boat far from home has a long trip ahead. When neither side has an edge, a compromise decides the order, and the one that goes first pays the other for its loss.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the direction carefully: the boat that is CLOSE to its destination gives way, and the far one goes first.
steps.whatToRemember: The double 'צדק' teaches two kinds of fairness: strict דין and fair פשרה. When neither side has a clear right, the court arranges a compromise with payment.

phrases.english: How is this done?
A loaded one and one that is not loaded –
the one that is not loaded gives way to the loaded one.
A close one and one that is not close –
the close one gives way to the one that is not close.
If both were close, or both were far –
impose a compromise between them,
and they pay a fee to each other.
phrases.notes: He means the one that goes first pays the one that waits for the loss of waiting.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and gives the practical rules for the boats and camels.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Loaded goes before unloaded, far goes before close, and if they are equal a compromise is made with payment.

steps.title: Seek out the best court of the generation
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא uses 'justice, justice you shall pursue' to teach that a person should go to the best בית דין, such as רבי אליעזר in לוד or רבן יוחנן בן זכאי in ברור חיל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'Justice, justice you shall pursue' means go after a fine בית דין: go after רבי אליעזר to לוד, and after רבן יוחנן בן זכאי to ברור חיל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new teaching. It uses the same פסוק to say that people should seek out the finest court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the word 'pursue' is read as an instruction to the people bringing the case. They should make the effort to travel to a great court, not just settle for any judge. The great rabbis of the time are given as examples.

keyTerms.meaning: The city where רבי אליעזר's court sat
The town where רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's court sat

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that pursuing justice is also the job of the people bringing the case: they should seek out the most qualified judges.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"Justice, justice you shall pursue" –
go after a fine court,
after Rabbi Eliezer to Lod,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי לִבְרוּר חַיִל.
phrases.english: after Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai to Beror Hayil.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: צֶדֶק צֶדֶק תִּרְדֹּף הַלֵּךְ אַחַר בֵּית דִּין יָפֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא that uses the same פסוק for a different lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should seek out the best court of the generation, like רבי אליעזר in לוד or רבן יוחנן בן זכאי in ברור חיל.

steps.title: Secret signals in בורני and ברור חיל
steps.stepSummary: A short teaching says that the sound of millstones in בורני meant a ברית מילה, and a burning lamp in ברור חיל meant a wedding feast.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: the sound of millstones grinding in בורני meant 'the week of the son, the week of the son.' The light of a lamp in ברור חיל meant 'a feast is there, a feast is there.'
steps.whatsHappening: The previous step mentioned ברור חיל, so the גמרא adds a side teaching about how people there signaled a happy event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These were signals people understood without anyone saying a word. Grinding meant a baby boy was born and a ברית was coming. A lit lamp meant there was a wedding. This is a side story and does not move the legal discussion forward.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (introduces a ברייתא-style teaching)
The week of the son: the celebration around a baby boy's ברית מילה
A feast, here a wedding feast

phrases.english: It was taught: the sound of millstones in Burni
meant: the week of the son, the week of the son.
phrases.notes: This means a baby boy was born and a ברית מילה was coming.

phrases.english: The light of a lamp in Beror Chayil
meant: a feast is there, a feast is there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side story set off by the mention of ברור חיל in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In בורני, millstone sounds signaled a ברית. In ברור חיל, a lit lamp signaled a wedding feast.

steps.title: Follow the great חכמים to their ישיבות
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'צדק צדק תרדף' as an instruction to follow the חכמים to their ישיבה. It then lists each great sage and the town where he taught.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'צדק צדק תרדף' means: go after the חכמים to their ישיבה. Go after רבי אליעזר to לוד, רבן יוחנן בן זכאי to ברור חיל, רבי יהושע to פקיעין, רבן גמליאל to יבנה, רבי עקיבא to בני ברק, רבי מתיא to Rome, רבי חנניה בן תרדיון to סיכני, רבי יוסי to ציפורי, רבי יהודה בן בתירה to נציבין, רבי יהושע to the גולה, רבי to בית שערים, and the חכמים to לשכת הגזית.
steps.whatsHappening: A second ברייתא uses the same פסוק as step 10. This time it gives a full list of great sages and the towns where each one taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 10 was about going to a good בית דין for a court case. This ברייתא says to go after the חכמים to their ישיבה, and it gives a much longer list of sages across the generations. The list ends with the greatest place of all, לשכת הגזית, where the חכמים sat in the time of the בית המקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: The academy or court where the sage sat
The Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the great סנהדרין sat in the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different 'רבי יהושע' in this list. The first is in פקיעין in ארץ ישראל. The second is in the גולה (בבל).

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: "Justice, justice shall you pursue"
phrases.notes: דברים 16:20

phrases.english: means: go after the Sages to the academy.
After Rabbi Eliezer to Lod,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי לִבְרוּר חַיִל,
phrases.english: after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to Beror Chayil,
after Rabbi Yehoshua to Peki'in,
after Rabban Gamliel to Yavneh,
after Rabbi Akiva to Bnei Brak,
after Rabbi Matya to Rome,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בֶּן תְּרַדְיוֹן לְסִיכְנִי,
phrases.english: after Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon to Sikhni,
after Rabbi Yosei to Tzippori,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה לִנְצִיבִין,
phrases.english: after Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira to Netzivin,
after Rabbi Yehoshua to the exile,
phrases.notes: Here 'the exile' means בבל.

phrases.english: after Rabbi to Beit She'arim,
phrases.notes: Plain 'רבי' with no name means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: after the Sages to the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״צֶדֶק צֶדֶק תִּרְדֹּף״ – הַלֵּךְ אַחַר חֲכָמִים לִישִׁיבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side story, this goes back to reading 'צדק צדק תרדף' and expands the short list from step 10.
steps.whatToRemember: 'צדק צדק תרדף' also teaches that a person should seek out the greatest חכמים of the generation, wherever they are.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק teaches that a person should follow the חכמים to their ישיבה.

steps.title: What does בית דין say when it opens a case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about how a case is opened and asks what words the judges actually use to open in favor of the accused.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: in money cases the judges open the discussion either way. In what words do we open it in favor of the accused?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the משנה and asks a practical question. This sets up רב יהודה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that in capital cases the judges must open with a point in favor of the accused. The גמרא wants to know what is actually said out loud. What would a 'point in favor' sound like when the evidence is witnesses?

keyTerms.meaning: How do we say it? (what words are used?)

phrases.english: Money cases are opened, etc.
phrases.notes: Only the start of the משנה is quoted. The rest says capital cases may be opened only in favor of the accused.

phrases.english: How do we say it?

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת פּוֹתְחִין כּוּ׳. הֵיכִי אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתות about 'צדק צדק תרדף' and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The actual words בית דין uses to open the discussion in favor of the accused.

steps.title: רב יהודה: ask the witnesses how they can be sure
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the judges open by asking the witnesses: 'Who says it happened the way you said?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: this is what we say to them: Who says it is the way you said?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question. The opening words are a challenge to the witnesses' testimony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point in favor of the accused is to raise doubt about the witnesses. Maybe they made a mistake or did not see clearly. Asking this opens the door to finding the accused not guilty.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
This is what we say to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the witnesses.

phrases.english: Who says it is as you said?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הָכִי אָמְרִינַן לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The judges open by asking the witnesses, 'Who says it happened as you said?'

steps.title: עולא: won't this scare the witnesses into silence?
steps.stepSummary: עולא objects that challenging the witnesses this way will shut them up.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said to him: But then we are silencing them!
steps.whatsHappening: עולא pushes back on רב יהודה's opening line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the judges start by doubting the witnesses, the witnesses may feel accused of lying. Then they may stop testifying, even when they are telling the truth. עולא thinks this is a bad way to open.

keyTerms.meaning: We silence or block them, like muzzling an animal

phrases.english: Ulla said to him:
But we are silencing them!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ עוּלָּא: וְהָא חָסְמִינַן לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's answer from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's opening line, 'Who says it is as you said?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Doubting the witnesses right away will scare them, and they will stop testifying.

steps.title: Let them be silenced: a ברייתא about moving witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that it is fine if the witnesses are silenced. A ברייתא shows that בית דין even moves witnesses from place to place to unsettle them, so that lying witnesses will back down.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let them be silenced! Wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אליעזר says, we move the witnesses from place to place so that their minds get confused and they take back their testimony?
steps.whatsHappening: עולא's challenge is answered: silencing the witnesses is not a problem. The answer is backed up by a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In capital cases, בית דין is happy to put pressure on witnesses. Witnesses who are lying will get confused and back down, while truthful witnesses will stay firm. רבי שמעון בן אליעזר teaches that judges even move witnesses on purpose to rattle them, so a sharp question at the start is surely fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Wasn't it taught in a ברייתא? (brings a proof)
We move them from place to place

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how strongly the court protects the accused in capital cases. בית דין may test witnesses hard, because the goal is to keep false testimony from taking a life.

phrases.english: So let them be silenced!
phrases.notes: This is רב יהודה answering עולא back.

phrases.english: Wasn't it taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Shimon ben Eliezer says,
we move the witnesses from place to place
so that their minds get confused and they take back their testimony?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers עולא's challenge from step 15 and supports רב יהודה from step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the result of the challenge and shows it is not a problem, backed by a ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Silencing the witnesses would be a flaw in רב יהודה's opening line.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pressuring witnesses in capital cases is acceptable and even intended, as the ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אליעזר shows.
steps.raayaObject: That בית דין may put pressure on witnesses even if it might silence them.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אליעזר about moving witnesses from place to place.

steps.title: Moving witnesses around is not the same as challenging them directly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the ברייתא about moving witnesses. In that case the witnesses lose their confidence on their own. Here the judges would be pushing them down directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are the cases really the same? There, the witnesses get pushed off by themselves. Here, we would be pushing them off with our own hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the answer from Step 16. It says the ברייתא about moving witnesses does not prove that judges may silence witnesses directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When witnesses are moved from place to place, any nervousness comes from the situation itself. Asking them 'Who says it happened that way?' is the court itself attacking them, and that is a different thing. So עולא's objection from Step 15 is back in force.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they really the same? (used to show two cases are different)
with our own hands, by direct action

phrases.english: Are they comparable?
phrases.notes: He is comparing the ברייתא about moving witnesses from Step 16 with רב יהודה's question to the witnesses.

phrases.english: There, they are pushed off by themselves,
here, we push them off with our own hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? הָתָם מִמֵּילָא קָא מִידְּחוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ברייתא about moving witnesses from place to place.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In the ברייתא the witnesses get shaken up on their own. In רב יהודה's version the court would be shaking them up directly.
steps.confusionAlert: This line does not say that moving witnesses around is wrong. It only says that case cannot support the court silencing witnesses directly.

steps.title: עולא's answer: ask the accused if he has witnesses to make them זוממין
steps.stepSummary: Since רב יהודה's answer was rejected, עולא gives a new version of what the judges say. They turn to the accused and ask whether he has witnesses who can make the first witnesses זוממין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, עולא said: This is what we say to the accused: 'Do you have witnesses to make them זוממין?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the question from Step 13 and gives a new answer from עולא. The judges' opening words are spoken to the accused, not to the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This avoids the problem of shutting the witnesses up, because the judges never challenge them directly. Instead the accused is invited to bring his own witnesses who will say the first witnesses were somewhere else at the time.

keyTerms.meaning: rather (drops the earlier answer and offers a new one)
proving witnesses were elsewhere at the time, which makes them עֵדִים זוֹמְמִין

phrases.english: Rather, Ulla said:
phrases.notes: This is the same עולא who objected in Step 15. Now he gives his own answer.

phrases.english: This is what we say:
"Do you have witnesses to show they are conspiring witnesses?"
phrases.notes: These words are said to the accused. The question is whether he has witnesses who can prove the first pair were somewhere else.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since Step 17 rejected the earlier answer, this offers a new answer to the question in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What words the judges use to open in favor of the accused.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They ask the accused: 'Do you have witnesses to make them זוממין?'

steps.title: רבה objects: helping the accused should not endanger the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks whether the court may open with something that helps the accused but brings punishment on the witnesses. If they are shown to be זוממין, the witnesses themselves could be punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to עולא: But do we open with something that is good for this one and bad for that one?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה challenges עולא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pointing toward הזמה does help the accused. But it also exposes the witnesses to the punishment of עדים זוממין. רבה assumes the court should not open the case with words that lead to someone else's liability.

keyTerms.meaning: his merit, what is in his favor
his liability, what is against him

phrases.english: Rabba said to him:
But do we open with the merit of this one
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the accused.

phrases.english: when it is the liability of that one?
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the witnesses, who could be punished as זוממין.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי פּוֹתְחִין בִּזְכוּתוֹ שֶׁל זֶה שֶׁהִיא חוֹבָתוֹ שֶׁל זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks עולא's answer in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's wording: 'Do you have witnesses to make them זוממין?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The court's opening should not help one person by putting another person in danger. הזמה would make the witnesses liable.

steps.title: Are the witnesses really in danger? זוממין are only killed after the verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רבה's worry using a משנה: עדים זוממין are not killed unless the verdict against the accused was already finished. At the opening of the case there is no verdict yet, so the witnesses would not be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is it really bad for the witnesses? Didn't we learn in a משנה: עדים זוממין are not killed until the verdict is finished?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבה's objection. It cites a משנה to show the witnesses would not actually be in danger at this early point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The punishment of עדים זוממין only applies if their lie already led to a final verdict. The opening words are said before any verdict. So it seems that proving them זוממין now could not lead to their death.

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't we learn in a מִשְׁנָה?
lying witnesses who are proven to have been elsewhere

phrases.english: But is it really his liability?
But didn't we learn in a mishna:
phrases.notes: This משנה is in מכות 5b.

phrases.english: Conspiring witnesses are not killed
until the verdict is finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's objection in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that asking about הזמה would make the witnesses liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה says עדים זוממין are only killed after the verdict is finished. At the opening of the case there is no verdict, so no liability.

steps.title: רבה explains: the accused might wait until after the verdict
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains what he meant. If the accused stays quiet until the verdict is finished and only then brings his witnesses to make them זוממין, the witnesses would be liable. So the question does lead to their liability in the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what I meant: If the accused stays quiet until his verdict is finished, and then brings witnesses and makes them זוממין, it ends up being bad for the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends his objection from Step 20's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the judges tell the accused that הזמה is an option, he could wait for the verdict to be finished. Then he brings his witnesses, and the first witnesses become fully liable as עדים זוממין. So the court's opening words would still lead to their punishment.

phrases.english: This is what I am saying:

phrases.aramaic: אִילּוּ שָׁתֵיק הַאי עַד דְּמִיגְמָר דִּינֵיהּ,
phrases.english: If this one would stay silent until his verdict is finished,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the accused.

phrases.english: and then brings witnesses and shows they are conspiring witnesses,
it would turn out to be the liability of that one.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אָמֵינָא: אִילּוּ שָׁתֵיק הַאי עַד דְּמִיגְמָר דִּינֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 20 and keeps רבה's objection from Step 19 standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains what the objection meant: a scenario where the danger comes later.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witnesses are safe, because the question is asked before any verdict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The accused could wait until after the verdict and then bring witnesses, so the witnesses would become liable.

steps.title: רבה's answer: ask the accused if he has witnesses to contradict them
steps.stepSummary: רבה gives his own wording. The judges ask the accused whether he has witnesses who contradict the first witnesses' story. When witnesses are only contradicted, nobody is punished, so no one is hurt by this question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבה said: We say to the accused: 'Do you have witnesses to contradict them?'
steps.whatsHappening: Since עולא's answer was rejected, רבה offers a new answer to the question from Step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הכחשה (contradicting the facts) is different from הזמה (saying the witnesses were elsewhere). If witnesses are only contradicted, the testimony falls away but the first witnesses are not punished. This helps the accused without endangering anyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: contradicting the witnesses' account of the facts

steps.whatToRemember: There are three versions of the opening words. רב יהודה: ask the witnesses (rejected, because it silences them). עולא: ask the accused about הזמה (rejected, because it can make the witnesses liable). רבה: ask the accused about הכחשה, which helps him and hurts no one.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up הזמה and הכחשה. הזמה attacks the witnesses themselves ('you were with us elsewhere') and punishes them. הכחשה only disputes the facts, and no one is punished.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabba said:
We say to him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the accused.

phrases.english: "Do you have witnesses to contradict them?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After עולא's answer is rejected in Steps 19–21, רבה offers his own answer to Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What words the judges use to open in favor of the accused.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They ask the accused: 'Do you have witnesses to contradict them?'
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the principle that the court's opening in favor of the accused must not create liability for anyone else.

steps.title: רב כהנא's wording: from your words he is acquitted
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא says the court opens by telling the witnesses that, based on their own words, the accused is acquitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: The judges say, "From your words, so-and-so is acquitted."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer to the same question: what words does the court use to open in favor of the accused? רב כהנא offers his version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's and רבה's wordings were spoken to the accused and asked whether he had witnesses. רב כהנא's wording is said to the witnesses and is a short opening announcement. It does not ask the accused to bring other witnesses, so the worry about the witnesses becoming זוממין does not come up.

keyTerms.meaning: From your words (said to the witnesses)
So-and-so (a stand-in for the accused's name)

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
"From your words, so-and-so is acquitted."
phrases.notes: This is said to the witnesses. The court opens by pointing toward acquittal, and then the real discussion begins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel answer to the same question that רבה answered in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exact words does the court use to open a capital case in favor of the accused?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court tells the witnesses: "From your words, so-and-so is acquitted."

steps.title: אביי and רבא's wording: if you did not kill, do not fear
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא both say the court tells the accused that if he did not kill, he has nothing to fear.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי and רבא both say: We say to him, "If you did not kill, do not be afraid."
steps.whatsHappening: Another wording for the opening line. אביי and רבא say the judges speak to the accused and calm him down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opening goes back to speaking to the accused, but it does not ask him about other witnesses. It simply tells him that an innocent man will be cleared. That encourages him to speak up for himself, and nobody is put at risk of punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: Be afraid (here: do not be afraid)

phrases.english: Abaye and Rava, who both say:
We say to him,
phrases.notes: "Him" means the accused.

phrases.english: "If you did not kill, do not fear."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another parallel answer, spoken to the accused, not to the witnesses as in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exact words open the case in favor of the accused?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court tells the accused: "If you did not kill, do not fear."

steps.title: רב אשי's wording: anyone who knows a merit should come forward
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the court announces that anyone who knows a point in the accused's favor should come and say it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The court announces, "Whoever knows a point in his favor should come and say it on his behalf."
steps.whatsHappening: A fourth wording. רב אשי says the opening is a public call for anyone who can help the accused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opening is spoken to everyone present, not to the witnesses or the accused. It invites any argument that helps him. Like the other new wordings, it starts the case on the side of acquittal without putting anyone in danger.

keyTerms.meaning: A point in someone's favor, a reason to acquit

steps.whatToRemember: Two wordings for opening in the accused's favor were rejected: רב יהודה's ("who says it is as you said?") because it silences the witnesses, and עולא's ("do you have witnesses to make them זוממין?") because it can make the witnesses liable. Four wordings stand: רבה ("do you have witnesses to contradict them?"), רב כהנא ("from your words so-and-so is acquitted"), אביי and רבא ("if you did not kill, do not fear"), and רב אשי ("whoever knows a merit, come forward").

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
"Whoever knows a point in his favor
should come and teach on his behalf."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last of the parallel wordings. This one is a public announcement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exact words open the case in favor of the accused?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A public call: "Whoever knows a point in his favor should come and argue for him."

steps.title: A ברייתא supports אביי and רבא: the סוטה verse opens with innocence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא backing אביי and רבא. רבי points out that the כהן's words to the סוטה begin with "if no man has lain with you."
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא is taught in line with אביי and רבא. רבי says: The verse says, "If no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone astray…"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof for אביי and רבא by starting to quote a ברייתא. The quote continues after this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the כהן speaks to the סוטה, he first describes the case where she is innocent. That matches אביי and רבא's "if you did not kill, do not fear," which also speaks to the accused person and first tells them that an innocent person will be cleared.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (in a ברייתא) in line with his view
A woman suspected of adultery who goes through the bitter-water ceremony

phrases.english: It is taught in accordance with Abaye and Rava.
Rabbi says:
"If no man has lain with you
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:19. These are the כהן's words to the סוטה.

phrases.english: and if you have not gone astray, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to step 24 and brings support for אביי and רבא's wording.
steps.raayaObject: אביי and רבא's wording: telling the accused, "If you did not kill, do not fear."
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי about the כהן's words to the סוטה (במדבר 5:19), which begin with the innocent case.
